3.0.0.en: The last days: after the Incarnation of Christ and His redemption, that is, in the New Testament.

3.0.1.en: The Apostle Paul warns his disciple of afflictions that will come about through the heretics. These began in the days of the Apostle, but they increased after that and continue until now. Anticipating a thing lessens its disturbance to a person when he meets it and makes him prepare for it, and this is the purpose of the Apostle Paul.

3.1.0.en: Men: he means the heretics and their followers, and also everyone who withdraws from the Church and the commandments of God. Here the Apostle mentions the kinds of evils into which people fall who are far from the Church or who follow the heretics, and they are:

3.1.1.en: 1- Lovers of their own selves: selfishness is the sin from which all the following sins result. Because the wicked person has withdrawn from the love of God, he turns to love of himself and consequently neglects his love for others.

3.1.2.en: 2- Covetous: when he thinks of himself he discovers his weakness, so he tries to strengthen himself with money and possessions, and because he is selfish he becomes greedy and avaricious in seeking money at the expense of those around him, and even makes light of breaking God's commandments in order to acquire money.

3.1.3.en: 3- Boasters, proud: the more money he acquires, the more he is proud of what he has acquired and thinks himself to be something, although he is a lowly slave to money, rejected by God and not loved by people.

3.1.4.en: 4- Blasphemers: whoever is occupied with himself, money and pride and is enslaved to them finds it easy to deny God and reject His commandments, and even reviles God, the Church and all the commandments with evil speech.

3.1.5.en: 5- Disobedient to parents: whoever has refused to submit to God and His love, the next step is rejecting the authority of parents and ingratitude toward them, even exploiting them, and insisting on his own opinion and not respecting their opinions and the opinions of elders and of all teachers.

3.1.6.en: 6- Unthankful: the one who rejects God and is attached to money is a complainer because he always feels wronged and that he deserves more than what he has. The more he is confined to selfishness and love of money, the more his complaining increases and his life becomes miserable.. because he does not enjoy the much that he has, unlike the contented and thankful person who lives with God, for God fills his heart with happiness.

3.1.7.en: 7- Unholy: when a person is separated from God he is left in an emptiness, so he easily falls into uncleanness of its various kinds, thinking that it will satisfy him. And the more he is absorbed in its lusts, the more thirst for them he feels, so he advances from evil to worse.

3.2.0.en: 8- Without natural affection: whoever is enslaved to selfishness will naturally be harsh in his speech and his dealings with others.

3.2.1.en: 9- Trucebreakers: as we mentioned, the one absorbed in material things cannot give thanks because they do not satisfy him and always lead him to complaining.

3.2.2.en: 10- False accusers: whoever falls into love of himself finds it easy to judge others because he sees only himself as sound in his conduct, so he readily ascribes the fault to others.

3.2.3.en: 11- Incontinent: the lover of money and of himself regards evil as permissible, and therefore he is not reliable in dealings and not pure in his heart.

3.2.4.en: 12- Fierce: the conduct of the selfish person is not only devoid of tenderness, but he is harsh, and as he persists in his harshness he becomes fierce in his dealings, troublesome to those around him.

3.2.5.en: 13- Despisers of those that are good: since they are occupied with material things, they neglect works of goodness, and with time they even mock them and reject them because they conflict with their evil material inclinations.

3.3.0.en: 14- Traitors: whoever is enslaved to love of himself and money does not love others, so it is easy for him to betray them, because he has betrayed God and rejected His commandments.

3.3.1.en: 15- Heady: they are not content with doing evil but are bold in seeking material things even if they wrong others, intrude into their lives and cause them much harm.

3.3.2.en: 16- Highminded: that is, proud, as we mentioned, because the further they persist in evil the more they increase in pride, so he repeats this quality once more.

3.3.3.en: 17- Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God: he concludes his words with the first quality with which he began, which is selfishness, which makes a person reject God and not love Him.

3.3.4.en: Each of these previous sins leads to the other, for they are a successive chain and one ring, bringing the wicked person back to where he began, to repeat throughout his life these entangled evils.

3.4.0.en: 18- Having a form of godliness: the last evil quality is hypocrisy, for they are not content with doing these entangled evils but cover them by pretending to be godly while in truth they are completely far from godliness, and by this hypocrisy they close the door of repentance before them, deluding themselves and some people that they are godly and so do not need repentance.

3.4.1.en: Paul charges his disciple to avoid these heretics and wicked people and to keep away from them so as not to be defiled by their ideas and conduct, and to be content with praying for them.

3.4.2.en: If you are falling into one of these sins, hasten to repent and to train yourself in the opposite virtue while clinging to God and the Church, and you will be freed from the slavery of sin.

3.5.1.en: Silly women: a diminutive of women, meaning to belittle them for their frivolity and their rush into evil, or meaning women young in age who are easily influenced.

3.5.2.en: The heretical teachers tried to spread their teachings and found willing ears among women because of their quick emotional response, so they would visit homes to spread their teachings, and some frivolous women accepted their teachings, and were even influenced by their personalities and became emotionally attached to them. And because the Gnostic heretics despise the body and believe it will not rise in the resurrection, they regarded fornication as permissible, and some women rushed into emotion with them until they fell into uncleanness. Thus they combined deviation of belief with evil also, by impurity.

3.5.3.en: Do not be lax with small sin, accepting an affection out of place or careless conduct with the opposite sex, lest you be drawn into it and fall into graver sins. And do not be deceived by the thoughts of the devil, who puts forward reasons for your wrong relationship as though it were a necessity that circumstances impose on you, but repent quickly and cut off every bad relationship, for the salvation of your soul is more important than everything.

3.6.0.en: These frivolous women, although they hear the teachings of the Church and the Christian teachers are concerned for them that they may return to the truth, are nevertheless led away by their lusts and their attachment to the heretical teachers, and consequently cannot accept the right teaching.

3.6.1.en: If you are insisting on a certain sin and regarding it as permissible, this will keep you from hearing the voice of God even if you enter the church every day. Therefore may you repent, and know that your weakness does not hinder you from hearing the voice of God as long as you strive and try, and trust that God will rescue you.

3.7.0.en: Jannes and Jambres: the chiefs of the magicians whom Pharaoh brought to resist Moses by turning their rods into serpents, but Moses' serpent swallowed up their serpents (Ex 7:8-13). Paul learned their names from the Jewish tradition handed down through the generations.

3.7.1.en: Resistance to the truth in all generations began with Satan's resisting Eve and continues until now, and Paul gives an example of these resisters, namely the magicians who were in the days of Moses. And he comments on the resisters in general, describing them as corrupt in mind, that is, deviating after evil thoughts that prevent them from accepting faith in God. So they are reprobate concerning the faith, because they insist on their evil thoughts and at the same time reject the faith.

3.8.0.en: They: the two magicians Jannes and Jambres.

3.8.1.en: Paul reassures Timothy that the evil of the heretics will be exposed and they will not be able to lead the believers in the Church astray, but God will show their folly before the believers so that they reject their beliefs, just as the inability of Jannes and Jambres was shown before Moses when Moses cast down his rod and it became a serpent, then they cast down their rods and they became serpents, and Moses' serpent swallowed up their serpents, and in the end they declared their inability before Pharaoh and said, "This is the finger of God" (Ex 8:19).

3.9.0.en: After the Apostle described the conduct of the wicked heretics, he shows Timothy the conduct of the children of God through his imitation of his teacher Paul. And here the importance of the tradition of the Church becomes clear, for the faith is not mere information written in books but a life handed down from the Fathers to the children, and Paul sets it out for his disciple in what follows:

3.9.1.en: 1- My doctrine: whether his public or private sermons that he spoke to Timothy or what his epistles contain, in which the details of the faith, salvation and the Christian life become clear.

3.9.2.en: 2- Manner of life: conduct, which is the practical application of the teachings, confirming their truth and showing how to apply them.

3.9.3.en: 3- Purpose: his aim, which is love of Christ and eternity.

3.9.4.en: 4- Faith: his holding fast to Christ and to his creed which he made clear in his teachings and in his confronting the heretics, and which appeared in practice in his encounters with people, especially in difficult situations.

3.9.5.en: 5- Longsuffering: in exhorting the people, especially the resisters, and rebuking them that perhaps they might repent, and in reaching out to those far away and persuading them to believe.

3.9.6.en: 6- Charity: which appeared toward those near and far, and in his concern for everyone in need and his being moved by what his children and his people suffer in all the churches in which he preached.

3.9.7.en: 7- Patience: in enduring the resistance of the wicked and the heretics and enduring all the hardships of the ministry and its physical and psychological pains.

3.10.0.en: 8- Persecutions: what he endured from resisters, whether Jews or Gentiles or heretics, for the sake of his holding fast to the upright faith.

3.10.1.en: 9- Afflictions: these include physical and psychological sufferings and the hardships of working with his own hands for his livelihood, some of which are mentioned in (2 Cor ch. 11). St. Paul gives examples of the sufferings he endured during his preaching in some countries, which Timothy knows, and they were severe persecutions, the harshness of which he expresses by saying "what persecutions I endured". But he adds the important truth, namely God's protection of him, because these persecutions aimed at doing away with him, but God rescued him and kept him to continue his preaching until this hour.

3.10.2.en: Do not be troubled by the sufferings you face, for God allows only what is within your capacity, and if they seem heavy upon you, trust that God bears them for you. And do not fear threats, for who can overcome you as long as God is with you?

3.10.3.en: So hold fast to your faith, your love and your ministry however much the wicked resist you, knowing that your labor is very precious in the eyes of God, and that all the saints endured for the sake of Christ, for this is the sign of following Christ, that you bear your cross for His sake.

3.11.0.en: The Apostle Paul declares an important truth, which is that the persecutions to which he was exposed must happen to everyone who lives with Christ, because the life of righteousness is contrary to the conduct of the wicked world and even exposes its evil, so the world resists the righteous and persecutes them in order to silence their voices that rebuke it. And since the righteous expect these persecutions, they are not troubled by them, especially as Christ supports them and bears their hardships for them, and even comforts them and gives them joy within the afflictions.

3.12.0.en: Seducers: these heretics deviate from the truth and even claim that what they say is the truth.

3.12.1.en: Deceiving, and being deceived: they lead people astray, and they themselves lose the ability to discern, so they too are led further astray than those they lead.

3.12.2.en: On the other hand, the heretics and the wicked who falsify the truth lose the ability to discern, so their deviation and error increase and they lead astray with them the people who follow them, and so they advance from evil to evil, because they reject Christ and fall into many sins, as the Gnostics proclaimed the baseness and perishability of the body and so regarded evil lusts as permissible.

3.12.3.en: The labors of striving are not heavy, because Christ bears them with you and gives you delight in His fellowship, and the persecutions that come upon you are all external and cannot touch your heart, which is filled with the love of Christ. So hold fast to Him and you will live in reassurance.

3.13.0.en: If the wicked heretics have been led away after their deviant ideas, Paul urges his disciple to stand firm in the sound teachings which he learned from him, confident and believing in their source, because Paul received them from Christ Himself.

3.14.0.en: From a child: for his Jewish mother Eunice taught him and made him know the words of the Holy Bible, and so did his grandmother Lois.

3.14.1.en: The holy scriptures: the books of the Old Testament.

3.14.2.en: Able to make thee wise: gives you wisdom.

3.14.3.en: What helped Timothy to stand firm in the faith was not only Paul's teachings but also what he learned from his mother and grandmother about the Holy Bible, whose aim in all its prophecies and types in the Old Testament is to prepare him for faith in Christ the Savior.

3.15.0.en: All scripture: includes all the books of the Old Testament and also most of the books of the New Testament that had been written by then.

3.15.1.en: Is given by inspiration of God: God who gave it by the Holy Spirit as a meaning in the minds of the writers of the Holy Bible, and they wrote it in their own language and expressions, and God guided them so that they would not err in anything.

3.15.2.en: For doctrine: guidance for life with God and conduct with people.

3.15.3.en: For reproof: when we sin, it pricks our hearts to repentance and return to God.

3.15.4.en: For correction: setting right our deviations and bringing us back to the right faith and sound conduct.

3.15.5.en: For instruction: by convicting our consciences and depriving us of some passing pleasures and urging us to spiritual striving and enduring hardships for the sake of repentance.

3.15.6.en: In righteousness: the aim of the Holy Bible is righteousness and a pure life with God, and this is different from the teachings of the world, which aim at obtaining positions and material things.

3.15.7.en: St. Paul calls his disciple Timothy to hold fast to the Holy Bible, which is necessary for his life, because it is the word of God that leads him in the life of righteousness, teaching him and supporting him, and if he strays, bringing him back to the love of God and the doing of good.

3.16.0.en: The man of God: the spiritual person whose only aim is God.

3.16.1.en: Perfect: the word of God leads him in the way of perfection.

3.16.2.en: He encourages him that the words of the Holy Bible lead him in the way of Christian perfection and make him always ready for doing good and keeping away from evil.

3.16.3.en: How great is the humility of God, who embodies Himself in words written in His book, to draw near to us and encourage us to live with Him. May we take care each day to read a portion of the Holy Bible, understand it and live by it, knowing that each time we read the words God will reveal to us in them new depths of His love, because God is rich and boundless and His words satisfy us all our days.

3.16.4.en: Paul's approaching departure and his closing news

4.0.0.en: I charge thee: I press the request upon you.

4.0.1.en: At the end of the last of the Apostle Paul's epistles, while he awaits the end of his life on earth, he reaffirms the request to his beloved disciple before God, who sees them both and who will judge them with all mankind and has prepared His Kingdom for them that they may be happy with Him. This shows the importance of the following commandments.

4.1.1.en: In season, out of season: with regard to the servant, he should not excuse himself from the ministry because of his troubles, and should seize every opportunity to draw souls to Christ, taking care to present the word at the best time for the hearer so that he may accept it.

4.1.2.en: Reprove: those who err, for their evils, that they may repent.

4.1.3.en: Rebuke: the hard-hearted and the unjust, that they may turn back from their wrongs and stop the evil.

4.1.4.en: Exhort: after he warns the unjust and those who treat evil as permissible, their hearts become ready to hear exhortation, that is, teachings aimed at the salvation of their souls.

4.1.5.en: With all longsuffering: bear with those who err and give them successive opportunities to repent, and be patient with their arguments and their rejection and their offenses against you and against others.

4.1.6.en: And doctrine: join longsuffering with explaining the truth and showing them their faults so that they may repent.

4.1.7.en: The Apostle asks him to persevere in preaching and evangelizing whatever his circumstances and the difficulties he meets, not excusing himself from the ministry because of any obstacles but trying to overcome them, as Paul preached despite his illness, even while being tried before Felix and while in prison in Rome, and calls everyone to faith, and if there is need to rebuke the wicked who treat evil as permissible, let him be firm and strong in his speech with them, and at the same time, if they respond, teach them with longsuffering, as Christ was longsuffering toward the scribes and Pharisees yet at the same time rebuked them and threatened them with woes (Mt 23), and as John the Baptist rebuked Herod, and John Chrysostom the Empress for her injustice.

4.2.0.en: Having itching ears: the itching of the ears is an expression for the ears of the wicked, which do not want to hear anything but what they desire, because of their insistence on evil.

4.2.1.en: He encourages his disciple to seize the opportunities of preaching and calling souls before they increase in their evil and refuse to hear words of exhortation, and because of their absorption in their lusts they look for teachers who do not rebuke them but tell them what pleases them so that they continue in their evil, and by this their deviation from Christ increases, and these false teachers even delude them that they are walking in the sound way and invent strange ideas that are nothing but fables and have no relation to the truth.

4.3.0.en: If the wicked reject the truth and insist on not hearing it, he asks his disciple in his pastoral care and ministry for the following:

4.3.1.en: Watch thou: be alert to the deviant and the false teachers, so that you may rebuke them that they may repent and teach the rest how to stand firm in the faith.

4.3.2.en: Endure afflictions: for the sake of Christ in the ministry, whatever sufferings you are exposed to, as the Apostle Paul endured many afflictions even to death.

4.3.3.en: Do the work of an evangelist: which is caring for all souls and persevering in teaching them and seizing every opportunity for ministry.

4.3.4.en: Make full proof of thy ministry: whether by preaching to those who have not heard, and visiting those far away, or by establishing the believers.

4.3.5.en: If your heart is kindled with the love of God, you will care for serving those around you and encouraging them to be bound to Christ and the Church, and if they refuse you will keep praying for them until God gives you new opportunities and in the end you win them to Christ. So do not be lax in your responsibilities, especially if those around you ask them of you, and offer your care and your love at all times.

4.4.0.en: I am now ready to be offered: in the Law of Moses, when they offered sacrifices to God they would pour wine over them, so Paul likens himself to wine poured out on the sacrifice of the ministry, that is, his life is poured out and ended for the sake of the service of God.

4.4.1.en: The time of my departure: he likens his life on earth to a ship moored to the shore, and the time of its release from its moorings has drawn near, that is, he expects his martyrdom to be near and his freedom from the bond of the material body and the departure of his spirit to God.

4.4.2.en: Paul feels that his life poured out in the ministry is almost finished and that he has drawn near to martyrdom, to be loosed from the bonds of the body and to ascend to God.

4.5.0.en: Paul senses the tender feelings of his disciple, whose eyes weep when he parts from him (2 Tim 1:

4.5.1.en: 4), so how will he bear the news of his departure from the world? Therefore he reassures him that he has striven and lived with Christ and expects to receive the heavenly crown. And this crown is prepared for Paul and for all believers, that is, for Timothy and all his people who hold fast to God. So Paul is not proud and does not boast here of his striving, but at the end of his life he reassures and encourages his disciple.

4.5.2.en: I have fought a good fight: it shows the importance of the spiritual striving in which he walked according to the teachings of the Church, and of course this was with the support of God's grace.

4.5.3.en: I have finished my course: it shows the importance of completing the striving and the pursuit toward the Kingdom and persevering in enduring the labors of worship and ministry.

4.5.4.en: I have kept the faith: Paul held fast to the upright faith despite the many heresies around him and the pressures of the persecutors, and faithfully handed on this faith to all to whom he preached.

4.5.5.en: There is laid up for me a crown of righteousness: the reward that God has prepared for His children who hold fast to the faith and strive against sin. And he says "laid up" and not "received", for he must continue his striving to the last moment of his life.

4.5.6.en: Shall give me: this crown is a grace from God and not a merit of anyone, for it is grace that supports the striver and gives him a reward of love from God, which is eternal life in the Kingdom.

4.5.7.en: At that day: the day of judgment.

4.5.8.en: The righteous judge: God is just, so that He rewards His striving children who hold fast to Him with heavenly happiness and rejects the wicked and casts them away from Him into eternal torment.

4.5.9.en: Them also that love his appearing: the striving believers who await with longing the coming of Christ, to live with Him forever.

4.5.10.en: Take courage in your striving against sin and when the afflictions of life meet you, because your God has prepared for you the Kingdom in which He will compensate you for all the labors of earth, and because of the greatness of the glories of the Kingdom, may you seize every opportunity to live with Him and hasten to repentance if you fall.

4.6.0.en: Paul longed to see Timothy before his departure to heaven, because he is his beloved disciple and in order to give him his last charges, and also to establish the believers in Rome after his departure. But we notice the tenderness of Paul's feelings, that he did not mention his approaching departure so as not to trouble the feelings of his beloved disciple, and he mentioned in the following verses another reason, which is that many had forsaken him.

4.7.0.en: Demas: one of Paul's disciples, mentioned in (Col 4:14, Phlm 24), but because of Nero's burning of Rome and his accusing the Christians of it, Paul was arrested and everyone connected with him was exposed to the danger of arrest, so Demas preferred to leave Paul to preserve his life. The reason may also have been his preoccupation with material matters concerning himself and his family, which the Apostle Paul expressed as the present world, so he left Paul in Rome and went to Thessalonica.

4.7.1.en: Crescens: he is mentioned only in this place and was also one of Paul's disciples, and he left most likely for a ministry on which Paul sent him to Galatia, a region in Asia Minor.

4.7.2.en: Titus: one of the disciples close to Paul, to whom he sent one of his epistles, and he is the bishop of Crete. And Paul sent him on a ministry to the city of Dalmatia, which lies northwest of Macedonia, that is, the northern region of the land of Greece, and this city is on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, which is the Gulf of Venice.

4.8.0.en: Luke: he is the writer of the Gospel that bears his name and also of the Book of Acts, and one of Paul's disciples who accompanied him on most of his journeys, and he remained with him despite the danger of the situation, serving him in his last imprisonment in Rome.

4.8.1.en: Mark: he accompanied Paul on his first missionary journey, but because of his leaving Paul at the city of Perga in Pamphylia, most likely because of an illness that befell him, Paul preferred not to take him on his second journey (Acts 15:38), and Barnabas disagreed with Paul on this matter, so Barnabas took Mark and went to preach in the island of Cyprus, and after Barnabas departed to heaven Mark went to preach in North Africa and Egypt. Paul felt his need of Mark, so he asked Timothy to bring him with him. This shows his love and trust toward Mark, for he wanted to establish the believers in Rome after his departure, and he relied in this on Timothy, Mark and Luke.

4.9.0.en: Tychicus: one of Paul's disciples (Acts 20:4, Titus 3:12), who was with Paul in his first imprisonment in Rome (Col 4:7), (Eph 6:21). Paul sent him to Ephesus to lead the Church in the place of Timothy its bishop, whom he summoned to come to him in Rome.

4.10.0.en: Troas: a port of Mysia on the Bosphorus gulf.

4.10.1.en: The cloak: it appears that Paul was in haste in his departure from Troas when he was staying with one of his disciples named Carpus, and perhaps the haste was because of a persecution he was exposed to there. And this shows his extreme poverty, for he had no cloak to wear and so needed this cloak. It also shows Paul's modesty and tenderness of feeling, for he did not want to burden those around him by asking them for a cloak, because he needed it on account of his old age, his bodily weakness and the sufferings of prison.

4.10.2.en: The books, but especially the parchments: they are made of papyrus, and some of the skins of animals were called parchments. They contain either some books of the Holy Bible or some of Paul's writings, and he most likely asked for them because of the Church's need of them in Rome, especially after his departure.

4.11.0.en: Alexander the coppersmith: he resisted the Apostle Paul and stirred up many against him, and Paul endured this with patience and did not try to take revenge on him but left the matter to God.

4.11.1.en: The Lord reward him: Paul remained in his love for Alexander and left the recompense to God. These words do not mean asking vengeance upon Alexander, but relying on God and leaving Him to teach him and discipline him for the salvation of his soul in the way He sees fit.

4.12.0.en: This is the reason for mentioning Alexander's evils, that is, to warn Timothy of him, because he resists everyone who preaches Christ, so naturally he will resist Paul's disciple, Timothy, in his preaching.

4.13.0.en: At my first answer: the Apostle Paul was exposed to a series of trials in his first imprisonment in Rome in the year 62 AD.

4.13.1.en: May it not be laid to their charge: here Paul's fatherhood appears, as he makes excuse for them in the weakness of their faith and love, and asks God to forgive them and not to count this weakness against them.

4.13.2.en: Paul declares with sorrow the dispersal of his disciples from him during his trials, but he forgives them for it.

4.14.0.en: That by me the preaching might be fully known: Paul's aim was the continuation of his preaching in Rome, for his remaining in prison was an opportunity to preach to everyone who came to him in prison, until the preaching of Christ spread throughout Rome.

4.14.1.en: The mouth of the lion: he means Nero or Satan.

4.14.2.en: The Holy Spirit supported Paul and spoke through his tongue, so he defended himself and they were content with imprisoning him instead of killing him at this time, although they ordered his death after a while.

4.15.0.en: Paul trusts that God is able to keep him in the midst of all these dangers, and even to keep his life from sin, which is what he means by the phrase "every evil work", until he reaches the eternal Kingdom.

4.16.0.en: Prisca and Aquila: Prisca is another name for Priscilla, the wife of Aquila, and they were bound to Paul in his ministry, especially since they practiced the same craft in which Paul was skilled, which is tentmaking, so they spent a long time with him, and it was an opportunity for spiritual discipleship and a bond of love. It appears that Priscilla was distinguished above her husband in faith and ministry, so Paul was not ashamed to put her before her husband in sending greetings to them, although this was contrary to the custom of that time of putting the man first and despising the woman. The household of Onesiphorus: one of Paul's disciples who helped him in the ministry and who has departed to heaven, so he asks Timothy to greet the members of his family who are bound to the Church, and they most likely served, carrying on the ministry of the head of the family who departed.

4.17.0.en: Erastus: one of Paul's disciples, who held the post of treasurer of the city of Corinth (Rom 16:23), and he continued to live and serve there.

4.17.1.en: Trophimus: one of Paul's disciples, who accompanied him on his second missionary journey and was with him in Jerusalem, and Paul was accused of having brought him into the temple of the Jews, and they arrested him for this reason. He fell somewhat ill in the city of Miletus, which is the port of Ephesus (Acts 20:15), so Paul sent him greetings with Timothy.

4.18.0.en: Paul repeats to Timothy that he should come quickly before the winter season, which could delay his journey because of winds and rains. Here too the tenderness of Paul's feelings appears, for he did not mention the reason for his insistence on hurrying to come, namely his approaching departure, so as not to wound the feelings of his beloved disciple. And he mentions greetings from some believers of the Church of Rome to Timothy, among them "Linus", who later became bishop of Rome.

4.19.0.en: He concludes the epistle by asking God's grace and Christ's presence for his beloved disciple, and this is the greatest thing in existence, that God accompany the life of His children, supporting and strengthening them.

4.19.1.en: Be gentle in your speech about others and with them, do not judge anyone, praise them for their virtues, and consider their feelings as much as you can, looking to God's mercy upon you, that you may be tender toward all.
